<Tip>
**Memory Aid: "BASH" Vernacular Design**—Basic structure (elevated on stilts), Adaptive openings (large windows, screens), Steep roof (rapid water shedding), Honest materials (nipa, bamboo, timber). Every element of the bahay kubo addresses a specific climate challenge; the design is optimization, not tradition for tradition's sake.
</Tip>

blocks.raw:
<Note>
The bahay kubo achieves thermal comfort without conditioning through integrated systems: elevated structure enables cool air to enter from below, large windows create cross-ventilation, steep roof exhausts heat from the peak, and sawali screens control solar gain while maintaining diffuse light. Modern "sustainable" passive design techniques are rediscovering these vernacular principles.
</Note>

blocks.raw:
<Warn>
**Critical Distinction**: Romanticizing bahay kubo as "authentic design" without understanding material constraints risks overlooking why modern materials were adopted. Nipa thatch requires constant maintenance, deteriorates in 5–10 years, attracts pests, and offers limited durability. Contemporary vernacular-inspired design learns climatic principles while using durable, maintainable materials. Uncritical traditionalism ignores legitimate material improvements.
</Warn>

blocks.raw:
<Callout>
The **bahay kubo** and **bahay na bato** represent centuries of indigenous climate adaptation. The bahay kubo's elevated stilts, steeply pitched nipa-thatched roof, large windows, and open floor plan achieve natural ventilation rates of 8–10 ACH without fans—matching mechanical systems while eliminating operational energy. Francisco Mañosa's assertion, "Everything started with the Nipa Hut," reflects the philosophical foundation of authentic Philippine tropical architecture and BERDE-aligned sustainable design.
</Callout>
